Existence of closed geodesics through a regular point on translation surfaces

Duc-Manh Nguyen and Huiping Pan and Weixu Su Address:  Duc-Manh Nguyen
IMB Bordeaux, CNRS UMR 5251
Université de Bordeaux,
351, Cours de la Libération, 33405 Talence Cedex, France Email address: [redacted-email] Address: Huiping Pan
Department of mathematics, Jinan University,
510632, Tianhe, Guangzhou, P. R. China Email address: [redacted-email] Address: Weixu Su
School of Mathematical Science, Fudan University,
200433, Shanghai, P. R. China Email address: [redacted-email]
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We show that on any translation surface, if a regular point is contained in some simple closed geodesic, then it is contained in infinitely many simple closed geodesics, whose directions are dense in ℝ​ℙ1\mathbb{RP}^{1}. Moreover, the set of points that are not contained in any simple closed geodesic is finite. We also construct explicit examples showing that such points exist on some translation surfaces. For a surface in any hyperelliptic component, we show that this finite exceptional set is actually empty. The proofs of our results use Apisa’s classifications of periodic points and of GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit closures in hyperelliptic components, as well as a recent result of Eskin-Filip-Wright.

Keywords: translation surfaces, simple closed geodesics, periodic points, orbit closure
AMS MSC2010: 37E35, 30F30

1. Introduction

Translation surfaces are flat surfaces with conical singularities such that the holonomy of any closed curve (not passing through the singularities) is a translation of ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. On such a surface, a natural question one may ask is whether there exists any simple closed geodesic that avoids singularities and passes through a given regular point. This question is particularly relevant in view of applications to the theory of billiards.

Throughout this paper, the translation surfaces we consider will be closed, and by closed geodesics we will mean those that do not pass through singularities. In the literature, Masur [21] proved that the set of directions in which there exist simple closed geodesics is a dense subset of ℝ​ℙ1≃ℝ/π​ℤ\mathbb{RP}^{1}\simeq\mathbb{R}/\pi\mathbb{Z}. Later, Bosheritzan-Galperin-Krüger-Troubetzkoy [8] improved Masur’s result, they proved that the set of tangent vectors that generate closed geodesics is dense in the unit tangent bundle of the surface (see also [22]). Vorobets [33, 34] proved that for any translation surface, almost every regular point on it is contained in infinitely many simple closed geodesics, whose directions are dense in ℝ​ℙ1\mathbb{RP}^{1}.

In this paper, we will show

Theorem 1.

On any translation surface, every regular point, except for finitely many, is contained in some simple closed geodesic.

Furthermore, we have

Theorem 2.

Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a translation surface. If a regular point on (X,ω)(X,\omega) is contained in some simple closed geodesic, then

  1. (i)

    it is contained in infinitely many simple closed geodesics {γn}n≥1\{\gamma_{n}\}_{n\geq 1}, whose directions are dense in ℝ​ℙ1\mathbb{RP}^{1};

  2. (ii)

    the union ∪n≥1γn\cup_{n\geq 1}\gamma_{n} is dense in (X,ω)(X,\omega).

Remark 1.1.

On any translation surface, a regular point being contained in a simple closed geodesic is equivalent to it being contained in the interior of some cylinder.

For translation surfaces in the hyperelliptic components, we show that the finite exceptional set mentioned in Theorem 1 is actually empty.

Theorem 3.

Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a translation surface in one of the hyperelliptic components ℋhyp​(κ)\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(\kappa) with κ∈{(2​g−2),(g−1,g−1)}\kappa\in\{(2g-2),(g-1,g-1)\} for g≥2g\geq 2. Then any regular point of (X,ω)(X,\omega) is contained in infinitely many simple closed geodesics.

It is not difficult to construct translation surfaces on which there exist regular points not contained in any simple closed geodesic (see Section 3). Thus the exceptional subset is not empty in general.

Outline

Here below we will give an outline of the proofs. All the definitions and necessary materials will be introduced in Section 2. It is worth noticing that, even though the statements of these theorems only concern one individual surface, their proofs use in an essential way the structure of its GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})-orbit closure.

  1. (1)

    The strategy to prove Theorem 1 is to show that any regular point in a translation surface (X,ω)(X,\omega) that is not contained in any simple closed geodesic is a “periodic point” in the sense of Apisa [4].

  2. (2)

    Theorem 2 is based on a result of Eskin-Mirzakhani-Mohammadi (see Theorem 2.2) which states that, given a translation surface with marked points (X,ω,{p1,…,pn})(X,\omega,\{p_{1},\dots,p_{n}\}), for any interval I=[a,b]⊂ℝ/2​πI=[a,b]\subset\mathbb{R}/2\pi with b≠ab\neq a, the sector {atrθ(X,ω,{p1,…,pn}):t>0,θ∈I}\{a_{t}r_{\theta}(X,\omega,\{p_{1},\dots,p_{n}\}):t>0,\theta\in I\} is equidistributed in the SL​(2,ℝ)\textup{SL}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit closure of (X,ω,{p1,…,pn})(X,\omega,\{p_{1},\dots,p_{n}\}), where at=(et00e−t)a_{t}=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}e^{t}&0\\ 0&e^{-t}\end{smallmatrix}\right) and rθ=(cos⁡θ−sin⁡θsin⁡θcos⁡θ)r_{\theta}=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{smallmatrix}\right).

  3. (3)

    For Theorem 3, we now assume that (X,ω)(X,\omega) belongs to some hyperelliptic component ℋhyp​(κ)\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(\kappa), with κ∈{(2​g−2),(g−1,g−1)}\kappa\in\{(2g-2),(g-1,g-1)\}. By Theorem 2 and Theorem 4.2, we only need to show that every periodic point pp in (X,ω)(X,\omega) is actually contained in at least one simple closed geodesic. Note that by a result of Apisa [3, 5], we have a complete list of all the possibilities for ℒ=GL​(2,ℝ)⋅(X,ω)¯\mathcal{L}=\overline{\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})\cdot(X,\omega)}.

    If ℒ=ℋhyp​(κ)\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(\kappa), then by [4, Theorem 1.5], pp must be a regular Weierstrass point of XX. It follows from Proposition 6.1 that pp is contained in a simple cylinder of (X,ω)(X,\omega). Thus the theorem is proved for this case. By a simple observation (cf. Lemma 4.5), this also yields the proof for the case that ℒ\mathcal{L} consists of translation covers of surfaces in another hyperelliptic component of lower genus. See Definition 2.8 for the notion of translation cover.

    If ℒ\mathcal{L} is a non-arithmetic eigenform locus in genus two then either pp is Weierstrass point, or the GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit closure of (X,ω,p)(X,\omega,p) contains a surface with one marked point (Y,η,q)(Y,\eta,q) where (Y,η)(Y,\eta) is a Veech surface and qq is a regular Weierstrass point of YY. Note that the latter case occurs only if ℒ\mathcal{L} is the golden eigenform locus (see [6]). In both cases, Proposition 6.1 allows us to conclude. By Lemma 4.5, this also yields the proof for the case ℒ\mathcal{L} arises from a non-arithmetic eigenform locus by a covering construction.

    Assume now that ℒ\mathcal{L} is a closed orbit, which means that (X,ω)(X,\omega) is a Veech surface. In this case the theorem follows from Proposition 7.4.

    Finally, assume that ℒ\mathcal{L} consists of translation covers (see Definition 2.8) of flat tori branched over two points. In this case, we will show that the GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})-orbit closure of (X,ω,p)(X,\omega,p) contains a surface with one marked point (Y,η,q)(Y,\eta,q), where (Y,η)(Y,\eta) is a Veech surface and q∈Yq\in Y is a regular point. We then use Proposition 7.4 and Lemma 4.4 to conclude.

2. Background

In this section, we recall the basic definitions and important results that are used in the proofs of the main theorems.

2.1. Stratum

A translation surface can be defined as a pair (X,ω)(X,\omega) where XX is a compact Riemann surface of genus g≥1g\geq 1 and ω\omega is a holomorphic one-form on XX. In this description, the singularities of the flat metric correspond to the zeros of the one-form. We will also consider translation surfaces with some regular marked points. In this situation, those regular points will be considered as zeros of order 00. Given an integer g≥2g\geq 2, let κ=(k1,…,kn)\kappa=(k_{1},\dots,k_{n}) be an integral vector where ki≥0,i=1,…,nk_{i}\geq 0,\;i=1,\dots,n, and k1+⋯+kn=2​g−2k_{1}+\dots+k_{n}=2g-2. Then the moduli space of translation surfaces (X,ω)(X,\omega) where ω\omega has nn zeros with orders given by κ\kappa will be denoted by ℋ⁡(κ)\mathcal{H}(\kappa). The space ℋ⁡(κ)\mathcal{H}(\kappa) will be called a stratum.

It is a well-known fact that ℋ⁡(κ)\mathcal{H}(\kappa) is a complex orbifold of dimension 2​g+n−12g+n-1. For any (X,ω)∈ℋ⁡(κ)(X,\omega)\in\mathcal{H}(\kappa), we choose a basis (γ1,…,γ2​g+n−1)(\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{2g+n-1}) of the relative homology group H1​(X,Σ,ℤ)H_{1}(X,\Sigma;\mathbb{Z}), where Σ\Sigma is set of zeros of ω\omega (including the ones of order 00). By a slight abuse of notation, for (X′,ω′)∈ℋ⁡(κ)(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime})\in\mathcal{H}(\kappa) close to (X,ω)(X,\omega), we will also denote by γi\gamma_{i} the corresponding element of H1​(X′,Σ′,ℤ)H_{1}(X^{\prime},\Sigma^{\prime};\mathbb{Z}), where Σ′\Sigma^{\prime} is the zero set of ω′\omega^{\prime}. Then the map

Φ:(X,ω)↦(∫γ1ω,…,∫γ2​g+n−1ω)∈ℂ2​g+n−1\Phi:(X,\omega)\mapsto(\int_{\gamma_{1}}\omega,\dots,\int_{\gamma_{2g+n-1}}\omega)\in\mathbb{C}^{2g+n-1}

is a homeomorphism from a neighborhood of (X,ω)(X,\omega) onto its image, thus defines a local chart for ℋ⁡(κ)\mathcal{H}(\kappa) near (X,ω)(X,\omega). The map Φ\Phi is called the period mapping, and the associated local coordinates are called period coordinates. For a thorough introduction to the subject, we refer to [22, 37].

2.2. Saddle connection and cylinder

A saddle connection of (X,ω)(X,\omega) is a geodesic segment for the flat metric defined by ω\omega ending at the zeros of ω\omega which does not contain any zero in its interior. A cylinder of (X,ω)(X,\omega) is an open subset of XX which is isometric to (ℝ/c​ℤ)×(0,h)(\mathbb{R}/c\mathbb{Z})\times(0,h), with c,h∈ℝ>0c,h\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}, and not properly contained in another subset with the same property. The parameters cc and hh are called the circumference and the height of the cylinder respectively. The isometric mapping from (ℝ/c​ℤ)×(0,h)(\mathbb{R}/c\mathbb{Z})\times(0,h) to (X,ω)(X,\omega) can be extended to a map from (ℝ/c​ℤ)×[0,h](\mathbb{R}/c\mathbb{Z})\times[0,h] to XX. The images of (ℝ/c​ℤ)×{0}(\mathbb{R}/c\mathbb{Z})\times\{0\} and (ℝ/c​ℤ)×{h}(\mathbb{R}/c\mathbb{Z})\times\{h\} under this map are called the boundaries or borders of the cylinder. Each boundary component is a concatenation of some saddle connections in the same direction. Note that the two boundary components are not necessarily disjoint as subsets of XX. A cylinder is called simple if each of its boundary components consists of a single saddle connection. Note that every simple closed geodesic is contained in a unique cylinder, and a cylinder is foliated by parallel simple closed geodesics.

2.3. GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})-action

There is a natural GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}) action on ℋ⁡(k)\mathcal{H}(k), which acts on (X,ω)∈ℋ⁡(κ)(X,\omega)\in\mathcal{H}(\kappa) by post-composition with the atlas maps for (X,ω)(X,\omega). More precisely, let {(Ui,ϕi)}i∈I\{(U_{i},\phi_{i})\}_{i\in I} be an atlas of charts for (X,ω)(X,\omega) which defines the translation surface structure, covering XX except the zeros of ω\omega (see §1.8 of [22]). Then for a∈GL​(2,ℝ)a\in\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}), a⋅(X,ω)a\cdot(X,\omega) is defined by the atlas {(Ui,a∘ϕi)}i∈I\{(U_{i},a\circ\phi_{i})\}_{i\in I}. In period coordinates, the action of aa is given by applying aa to each coordinate (here, we use the standard identification ℂ≃ℝ2\mathbb{C}\simeq\mathbb{R}^{2}).

There is a deep connection between the dynamics of GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}) on ℋ⁡(κ)\mathcal{H}(\kappa) and the dynamics of straight line flows on individual translation surfaces. In more concrete terms, the geometric and dynamical properties of a translation surface is often encoded in its GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})-orbit closure in moduli space.

We recall the recent breakthroughs of Eskin-Mirzakhani ([11]) and Eskin-Mirzakhani-Mohammadi ([12]). Define an affine invariant submanifold ℳ\mathcal{M} in a stratum to be an immersed submanifold which is defined locally by homogeneous linear equations with real coefficients in the period coordinates (see [12] and [35] for more details).

Theorem 2.1 ([12]).

The GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit closure of any translation surface is an affine invariant submanifold in its stratum. Any GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}) invariant, closed subset of a stratum is a finite union of affine invariant submanifolds.

Note that each stratum is itself a GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})-orbit closure, by ergodicity of Teichmüller geodesic flow ([20]). A surface whose GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit is dense in its stratum is called generic. The above result of Eskin-Mirzakhani-Mohammadi is followed by further results by Avila-Eskin-Möller [1], Wright [35, 36], Filip [13] that provide more information about the orbit closures. However, obtaining the complete classification of GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})-orbit closures for each stratum remains a major challenge in Teichmüller dynamics.

Let at=(et00e−t)a_{t}=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}e^{t}&0\\ 0&e^{-t}\end{smallmatrix}\right) and rθ=(cos⁡θ−sin⁡θsin⁡θcos⁡θ)r_{\theta}=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{smallmatrix}\right). Let ℋ1​(κ)⊂ℋ​(κ)\mathcal{H}_{1}(\kappa)\subset\mathcal{H}(\kappa) be the set of translation surfaces of area one. The following theorem describes the equidistribution of sectors.

Theorem 2.2 (Theorem 2.6 in [12]).

Let (X,ω)∈ℋ1​(κ)(X,\omega)\in\mathcal{H}_{1}(\kappa) be a translation surface of are one. Let ℒ⊂ℋ1​(κ)\mathcal{L}\subset\mathcal{H}_{1}(\kappa) be the SL​(2,ℝ)\textup{SL}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit closure of (X,ω)(X,\omega). Then for any interval I=[a,b]⊂ℝ/2​πI=[a,b]\subset\mathbb{R}/2\pi with b≠ab\neq a, the sector {atrθ⋅(X,ω):t>0,θ∈I}\{a_{t}r_{\theta}\cdot(X,\omega):t>0,\theta\in I\} is equidistributed in ℒ\mathcal{L}.

Remark 2.3.

Theorem 2.2 also holds for translation surfaces with any number of regular marked points.

2.4. Veech surfaces

For a translation surface (X,ω)(X,\omega), let Aff​(X,ω)\textup{Aff}(X,\omega) be the group of orientation-preserving self-homeomorphisms of XX which are given by affine maps in the local charts defined by ω\omega. Elements of Aff​(X,ω)\textup{Aff}(X,\omega) are called affine automorphisms of (X,ω)(X,\omega) (see [15, 17, 22]). To each affine automorphism f∈Aff​(X,ω)f\in\textup{Aff}(X,\omega), one can associate a matrix a​(f)∈SL​(2,ℝ)a(f)\in\textup{SL}(2,\mathbb{R}) which is the derivative of ff in the local charts defined by ω\omega, i.e. the linear part of ff. The image of Aff​(X,ω)\textup{Aff}(X,\omega) in SL​(2,ℝ)\textup{SL}(2,\mathbb{R}) under the map f↦a⁡(f)f\mapsto a(f) is called the Veech group of (X,ω)(X,\omega), denoted by SL​(X,ω)\textup{SL}(X,\omega). The group SL​(X,ω)\textup{SL}(X,\omega) is also the stabilizer of (X,ω)(X,\omega) under the action of SL​(2,ℝ)\textup{SL}(2,\mathbb{R}). If SL​(X,ω)\textup{SL}(X,\omega) is a lattice of SL​(2,ℝ)\textup{SL}(2,\mathbb{R}), i.e. SL​(2,ℝ)/SL​(X,ω)\textup{SL}(2,\mathbb{R})/\textup{SL}(X,\omega) has finite volume with respect to the Haar measure on SL​(2,ℝ)\textup{SL}(2,\mathbb{R}), then (X,ω)(X,\omega) is called a Veech surface (or lattice surface).

Theorem 2.4 ([31, 32]).

A translation surface is a Veech surface if and only if its GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit is closed.

Since the parallel transport on a translation surface does not change the directions of the tangent vectors, for any direction θ∈ℝ​ℙ1\theta\in\mathbb{RP}^{1}, we have a (singular) foliation of the surface whose leaves are geodesics in this direction. This foliation is said to be uniquely ergodic if each of its leaves is dense and there is a unique transverse measure up to a multiplicative constant. On the other hand, this foliation is said to be periodic if each of its leaves is either a saddle connection or a closed geodesic. Veech surfaces are of particular interest because they have more “symmetries” than other surfaces. Moreover, they have optimal dynamical behaviors. Namely, we have

Theorem 2.5 ([32] Veech dichotomy).

Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a Veech surface, then for every direction, the directional flow is either periodic or uniquely ergodic.

As a consequence, we get

Corollary 2.6.

On a Veech surface, the direction of any saddle connection is periodic.

2.5. Hyperelliptic components

By Kontsevich-Zorich’s result ([19]), each stratum ℋ⁡(κ)\mathcal{H}(\kappa) has at most three connected components. If κ=(2​g−2)\kappa=(2g-2) or (g−1,g−1)(g-1,g-1), then ℋ⁡(κ)\mathcal{H}(\kappa) contains a special called hyperelliptic component, which will be denoted by ℋhyp​(κ)\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(\kappa). Let us describe ℋhyp​(κ)\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(\kappa) in details.

For g≥2g\geq 2, let 𝒬⁡(−4+ℓ,−1ℓ)\mathcal{Q}(-4+\ell,-1^{\ell}) be the set of meromorphic quadratic differentials on the Riemann sphere with one zero of order −4+ℓ-4+\ell and ℓ\ell simple poles, where ℓ=2​g+1\ell=2g+1 if κ=(2​g−2)\kappa=(2g-2), or 2​g+22g+2 if κ=(g−1,g−1)\kappa=(g-1,g-1). Then every translation surface in ℋhyp​(κ)\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(\kappa) is the holonomy double cover of a quadratic differential in 𝒬⁡(−4+ℓ,−1ℓ)\mathcal{Q}(-4+\ell,-1^{\ell}). The involution of (X,ω)(X,\omega) induced by the double cover is the hyperelliptic involution of XX.

For g=1g=1, by convention, we consider a flat torus with one or two marked points as a hyperelliptic translation surface and denote the corresponding strata by ℋ⁡(0)\mathcal{H}(0) and ℋ⁡(0,0)\mathcal{H}(0,0) respectively. Surfaces in ℋ⁡(0)\mathcal{H}(0) (resp. in ℋ⁡(0,0)\mathcal{H}(0,0)) are holonomy double covers of quadratic differentials in 𝒬⁡(−14)\mathcal{Q}(-1^{4}) (resp. 𝒬⁡(0,−14)\mathcal{Q}(0,-1^{4})).

All Riemann surfaces of genus two are hyperelliptic, and the strata ℋ⁡(2)\mathcal{H}(2) and ℋ⁡(1,1)\mathcal{H}(1,1) only contain hyperelliptic components. The following classification theorem of GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})-orbit closures of translation surfaces in genus two was obtained by McMullen, prior to the works of Eskin-Mirzakhani and Eskin-Mirzakhani-Mohammadi (parts of this classification were also obtained by Calta [9]). In this paper, we will denote the complex dimension of an orbit closure ℒ\mathcal{L} by dimℒ\dim\mathcal{L}. All dimensions we mention are complex dimensions.

Theorem 2.7 (McMullen [25, 24, 23]).

Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a translation surface in genus two, and let ℒ\mathcal{L} be the closure of its GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit in the corresponding stratum. If (X,ω)∈ℋ⁡(2)(X,\omega)\in\mathcal{H}(2), then either

  • (1-a)

    ℒ=ℋ⁡(2)\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{H}(2), or

  • (1-b)

    ℒ=GL​(2,ℝ)⋅(X,ω)\mathcal{L}=\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})\cdot(X,\omega); in this case, the Jacobian Jac​(X)\textup{Jac}(X) of XX admits real multiplication by a quadratic order of discriminant DD with ω\omega as an eigenform.

If (X,ω)∈ℋ⁡(1,1)(X,\omega)\in\mathcal{H}(1,1), then one of the following possibilities holds:

  • (2-a)

    ℒ=ℋ⁡(1,1)\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{H}(1,1).

  • (2-b)

    ℒ\mathcal{L} is contained in the locus of pairs (X,ω)(X,\omega) such that Jac​(X)\textup{Jac}(X) admits real multiplication by a quadratic order of discriminant DD with ω\omega as an eigenform, and dimℒ=3\dim\mathcal{L}=3.

  • (2-c)

    ℒ=GL​(2,ℝ)⋅(X,ω)\mathcal{L}=\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})\cdot(X,\omega); in this case ℒ\mathcal{L} must be contained in an orbit closure of the type described in (2-b).

We refer to [25] for the precise definitions. Orbit closures of the type (2-b) are called eigenform loci in ℋ⁡(1,1)\mathcal{H}(1,1) and indexed by the discriminant DD. If D=d2D=d^{2} for some integer dd, then the locus is called arithmetic, otherwise it is called non-arithmetic. In [24], McMullen showed that a non-arithmetic eigenform locus of type (2-b) and discriminant D≠5D\neq 5 does not contain any closed GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit. For D=5D=5, the corresponding eigenform locus, which is called the golden eigenform locus, contains a unique closed GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit.

Definition 2.8 (Translation cover).

Let (X1,ω1),(X2,ω2)(X_{1},\omega_{1}),(X_{2},\omega_{2}) be two translation surfaces. If there exists a (branched) cover π:X1→X2\pi:X_{1}\to X_{2} such that ω1=π∗​ω2\omega_{1}=\pi^{*}\omega_{2}, then (X1,ω1)(X_{1},\omega_{1}) is called a translation cover of (X2,ω2)(X_{2},\omega_{2}). In the case where (X2,ω2)(X_{2},\omega_{2}) is a flat torus, (X1,ω1)(X_{1},\omega_{1}) is called a torus cover.

Whenever we mention a (branched) cover in this paper, we mean a translation cover.

Recently, using the results of [11] and [12] together with technical tools developed in [26, 27], Apisa obtained the following classification of GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit closures in the hyperelliptic components of any genus.

Theorem 2.9 ([3, 5]).

Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a translation surface in some hyperelliptic component ℋhyp​(2​g−2)\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(2g-2) or ℋhyp​(g−1,g−1)\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(g-1,g-1), and ℒ\mathcal{L} the corresponding GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit closure. Then ℒ\mathcal{L} is one of the followings:

  1. (1)

    If dimℒ=2\dim\mathcal{L}=2, then ℒ\mathcal{L} is a closed orbit, i.e. (X,ω)(X,\omega) is a Veech surface.

  2. (2)

    If dimℒ=3\dim\mathcal{L}=3 and ℒ\mathcal{L} is arithmetic, that is ℒ\mathcal{L} is locally defined by linear equations with rational coefficients in period coordinates, then ℒ\mathcal{L} is a branched covering construction over ℋ⁡(0,0)\mathcal{H}(0,0).

  3. (3)

    If dimℒ=3\dim\mathcal{L}=3 and ℒ\mathcal{L} is nonarithmetic, then ℒ\mathcal{L} is a branched covering construction over some non-arithmetic eigenform locus in ℋ⁡(1,1)\mathcal{H}(1,1).

  4. (4)

    If dimℒ=2​r\dim\mathcal{L}=2r with 1<r<g1<r<g, then ℒ\mathcal{L} is a branched covering construction over ℋh​y​p​(2​r−2)\mathcal{H}^{hyp}(2r-2).

  5. (5)

    If dimℒ=2​r+1\dim\mathcal{L}=2r+1 with 1<r<g1<r<g, then ℒ\mathcal{L} is a branched covering construction over ℋh​y​p​(r−1,r−1)\mathcal{H}^{hyp}(r-1,r-1).

  6. (6)

    ℒ\mathcal{L} is the whole stratum.

The covers are branched over zeros of the holomorphic one-forms and commute with the hyperelliptic involution.

Remark 2.10.
  • •

    In genus three, this classification was obtained by Nguyen-Wright [30] and Aulicino-Nguyen [2].

  • •

    The classification of Veech surfaces (Teichmüller curves) remains open, even in genus two.

2.6. Marked points and periodic points

A point pp on a translation surface (X,ω)(X,\omega) is called regular if it is not a zero of ω\omega. A regular point pp on (X,ω)(X,\omega) is called a periodic point if the orbit closures GL​(2,ℝ)⋅(X,ω,p)¯\overline{\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})\cdot(X,\omega,p)} in ℋ⁡(κ,0)\mathcal{H}(\kappa,0) and GL​(2,ℝ)⋅(X,ω)¯\overline{\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})\cdot(X,\omega)} in ℋ⁡(κ)\mathcal{H}(\kappa) have the same dimension ([4, 6, 7, 14, 28]). For a Veech surface, this is equivalent to saying that the orbit of pp under Aff​(X,ω)\textup{Aff}(X,\omega) is finite.

When (X,ω)(X,\omega) is a surface in some hyperelliptic component, we have the following result for the periodic points of (X,ω)(X,\omega), due to Apisa and Möller.

Theorem 2.11 ([4, 6, 28]).

Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a primitive translation surface in some hyperelliptic component ℋh​y​p​(κ)\mathcal{H}^{hyp}(\kappa), where κ=(2​g−2)\kappa=(2g-2) or (g−1,g−1)(g-1,g-1).

  1. (1)

    If GL​(2,ℝ)⋅(X,ω)¯=ℋh​y​p​(κ)\overline{\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})\cdot(X,\omega)}=\mathcal{H}^{hyp}(\kappa), then the set of periodic points of (X,ω)(X,\omega) are the set of regular Weierstrass points.

  2. (2)

    If (X,ω)(X,\omega) is a primitive Veech surface of genus two, then the set of periodic points of (X,ω)(X,\omega) are the set of regular Weierstrass points.

  3. (3)

    If (X,ω)∈ℋh​y​p​(1,1)(X,\omega)\in\mathcal{H}^{hyp}(1,1) contains a periodic point pp which is not a Weierstrass point, then GL​(2,ℝ)⋅(X,ω)¯\overline{\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})\cdot(X,\omega)} is the golden eigenform locus.

Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a generic surface in the golden eigenform locus (cf. Section 2.5), and p∈(X,ω)p\in(X,\omega) be a periodic point which is not a Weierstrass point. Then it is shown in [6, §2] (see also [18]) that the GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit closure of (X,ω,p)(X,\omega,p) in ℋ⁡(1,1,0)\mathcal{H}(1,1,0) contains a translation surface with one marked point (Y,η,q)(Y,\eta,q), where (Y,η)(Y,\eta) is a Veech surface and qq is a regular Weierstrass point.

3. Existence of regular points not contained in any simple closed geodesic

In this section, we will give a family of translation surfaces which have regular points not contained in any simple closed geodesic.

Proposition 3.1.

Let (Y,q)(Y,q) be a meromorphic quadratic differential that has exactly one simple pole (the other singularities are zeros). Let π:(X,ω2)→(Y,q)\pi:(X,\omega^{2})\to(Y,q) be the holonomy double cover. Then the pre-image of the simple pole under the double cover is not contained in any simple closed geodesic.

Proof.

Let y∈Yy\in Y be the unique simple pole, and y~∈X\tilde{y}\in X be its preimage under the double cover π\pi. Let ii be the involution of XX that permutes the the sheets of the cover π\pi. It is clear that y~\tilde{y} is the only regular point which is invariant under ii. Suppose to a contradiction that y~\tilde{y} is contained in some simple closed geodesic, say γ\gamma. Then γ\gamma is invariant under the involution ii. Since orientation-reversing isometries of the circle have exactly two fixed points, there exists another fixed point of ii which is contained in γ\gamma. This contradicts the fact that y~\tilde{y} is the only non-singular fixed point of ii. ∎

Remark 3.2.
  • (i)

    With the above notation, if (Y,q)(Y,q) has the property that every regular point is contained in a simple closed geodesic, then y~=π−1​(y)\tilde{y}=\pi^{-1}(y) is the unique regular point of (X,ω)(X,\omega) that is not contained in any simple closed geodesic.

  • (ii)

    Let 𝒬\mathcal{Q} be the stratum of (Y,q)(Y,q). Combined with Theorem 4.2 below and [7, Th. 1.4], Proposition 3.1 implies that if 𝒬\mathcal{Q} does not consist entirely of hyperelliptic surfaces, and (Y,q)(Y,q) is generic in 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, then the preimage of the simple pole of qq is the unique regular point in XX which is not contained in any simple closed geodesic.

To close this section, we construct an explicit surface, which is square-tiled, on which there is a unique regular point that is not contained in any simple closed geodesic.

Example 1.

Consider the example (X,ω)(X,\omega) in Figure 1. It is obtained from a central symmetric polygon 𝒫\mathcal{P} via edges identification. It is a translation surface in ℋ⁡(1,1,1,1,2)\mathcal{H}(1,1,1,1,2), tiled by 40 squares. It is also a branched double cover over a quadratic differential (Y,q)∈𝒬⁡(1,2,2,−1)(Y,q)\in\mathcal{Q}(1,2,2,-1).

Let O∈(X,ω)O\in(X,\omega) be the point represented by the center of the polygon which is the preimage of the simple pole of qq. By Proposition 3.1, OO is a not contained in any simple closed geodesic of (X,ω)(X,\omega). Moreover, in this case, any other regular point is contained in some simple closed geodesic of (X,ω)(X,\omega). Indeed, by identification, the vertices of the squares are partitioned into 34 equivalence classes (two vertices belong to the same equivalence class if and only if they represent the same point on (X,ω)(X,\omega)). Five of them are the zeros of ω\omega, and the remaining 29 classes are regular points of ω\omega which are marked out in the figure. The center OO is one of these 29 regular points. Consider the eight cylinders on (X,ω)(X,\omega) which are the images of the two cylinders in Figure 1 under the x-reflection and y-reflection. It is not difficult to see that the remaining 28 noncenter regular points are contained in the interior of these eight cylinders. Any other regular point which is not a vertex of the unit square is contained in one of the horizontal or vertical cylinders.

4. Proof of Theorem 1

Our goal in this section is to prove Theorem 1.

4.1. Torus with marked points

Lemma 4.1.

Let (𝕋,p1,⋯,pk)∈ℋ⁡(0k)(\mathbb{T},p_{1},\cdots,p_{k})\in\mathcal{H}(0^{k}) be a torus with k≥1k\geq 1 marked points.

  • (1)

    If 1≤k≤21\leq k\leq 2, then every point p∈𝕋\{p1,⋯,pk}p\in\mathbb{T}\backslash\{p_{1},\cdots,p_{k}\} is contained in some simple closed geodesic of 𝕋\{p1,⋯,pk}\mathbb{T}\backslash\{p_{1},\cdots,p_{k}\}.

  • (2)

    If k≥3k\geq 3, then every regular point in 𝕋\{p1,⋯,pk}\mathbb{T}\backslash\{p_{1},\cdots,p_{k}\}, except for a finite set, is contained in some simple closed geodesic.

Proof.

Without loss of generality, we may assume that 𝕋\mathbb{T} is obtained by identifying the opposite sides of [0,1]×[0,1][0,1]\times[0,1] such that pp corresponds to (0,0)(0,0), and pi=(ai,bi)≠(0,0)∈[0,1]×[0,1]p_{i}=(a_{i},b_{i})\neq(0,0)\in[0,1]\times[0,1], 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k.

(1) 1≤k≤21\leq k\leq 2. It suffices to prove the statement for the case k=2k=2. Consider the following three simple closed geodesics through pp: the horizontal geodesic γ1\gamma_{1}, the vertical geodesic γ2\gamma_{2}, and the geodesic γ3\gamma_{3} with slope one. At least one of these three simple closed geodesics does not intersect {p1,p2}\{p_{1},p_{2}\}.

(2) k≥3k\geq 3. Let HH (resp. VV) be the union of all the horizontal (resp. vertical) simple closed geodesics passing through p1,…,pkp_{1},\dots,p_{k}. Then every point in 𝕋∖(H∩V)\mathbb{T}\setminus(H\cap V) is contained in at least one simple closed geodesic γ\gamma which dose not intersect {p1,…,pk}\{p_{1},\dots,p_{k}\}. Since H∩VH\cap V is a finite set, this completes the proof. ∎

4.2. Periodic points

Theorem 4.2.

Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a translation surface. Then any regular point which is not contained in any simple closed geodesic is a periodic point of (X,ω)(X,\omega).

As a consequence of Theorem 4.2, we get

Corollary 4.3.

Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a generic surface in a non-hyperelliptic component. Then every regular point of (X,ω)(X,\omega) is contained in some simple closed geodesic.

Proof.

By a result of Apisa [4, Cor.1], (X,ω)(X,\omega) does not have any periodic point. Thus, the corollary follows immediately from Theorem 4.2. ∎

Let ℒ=GL​(2,ℝ)⋅(X,ω)¯\mathcal{L}=\overline{\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})\cdot(X,\omega)}, and ℒ∗\mathcal{L}^{*} the set of translation surfaces with one marked point (Y,η,q)(Y,\eta,q), where (Y,η)∈ℒ(Y,\eta)\in\mathcal{L} and q∈(Y,η)q\in(Y,\eta) is a regular point. Let 𝒩⊂ℒ∗\mathcal{N}\subset\mathcal{L}^{*} be the set of translation surfaces with one marked point (Y,η,q)∈ℒ∗(Y,\eta,q)\in\mathcal{L}^{*} such that q∈(Y,η)q\in(Y,\eta) is not contained in any simple closed geodesic.

Lemma 4.4.

The subset 𝒩\mathcal{N} is GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}) invariant, closed, and proper.

Proof.

It is clear that 𝒩\mathcal{N} is GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}) invariant. The properness follows from Masur’s result ([21]) that (X,ω)(X,\omega) contains infinitely many simple closed geodesics. To prove that 𝒩\mathcal{N} is closed, it suffices to prove that its complement 𝒩c\mathcal{N}^{c} is open. Let (Y,η,q)(Y,\eta,q) be an element of 𝒩c\mathcal{N}^{c}. Then qq is contained in at least one simple closed geodesic of (Y,η)(Y,\eta), which implies that qq is contained in the interior of at least one cylinder. This cylinder persists on nearby surfaces in ℒ∗\mathcal{L}^{*}. As a consequence, for all surfaces (Y′,η′,q′)(Y^{\prime},\eta^{\prime},q^{\prime}) sufficiently close to (Y,η,q)(Y,\eta,q), q′q^{\prime} is contained in at least one simple closed geodesic of (Y′,η′)(Y^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}). Therefore, 𝒩c\mathcal{N}^{c} is open in ℒ∗\mathcal{L}^{*}. ∎

Proof of Theorem 4.2.

Let ℒp⊂𝒩\mathcal{L}_{p}\subset\mathcal{N} be the GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit closure of (X,ω,p)(X,\omega,p) in ℒ∗\mathcal{L}^{*}. By Lemma 4.4, ℒp\mathcal{L}_{p} is a proper affine invariant submanifold of ℒ∗\mathcal{L}^{*}. Therefore, dimℒ≤dimℒp<dimℒ∗=dimℒ+1\dim\mathcal{L}\leq\dim\mathcal{L}_{p}<\dim\mathcal{L}^{*}=\dim\mathcal{L}+1. Hence, dimℒ=dimℒp\dim\mathcal{L}=\dim\mathcal{L}_{p} and, by definition, pp is a periodic point of (X,ω)(X,\omega). ∎

4.3. Proof of Theorem 1

Lemma 4.5.

Let (X1,ω1),(X2,ω2)(X_{1},\omega_{1}),(X_{2},\omega_{2}) be two translation surfaces, and π:(X1,ω1)→(X2,ω2)\pi:(X_{1},\omega_{1})\to(X_{2},\omega_{2}) a translation cover. Let Σ2\Sigma_{2} be the finite subset of X2X_{2} that contains all the zeros of ω2\omega_{2} and the images of the branched points of π\pi. Let Σ1=π−1​(Σ2)\Sigma_{1}=\pi^{-1}(\Sigma_{2}). Assume that any point in X2\Σ2X_{2}\backslash\Sigma_{2} is contained in some simple closed geodesic which does not intersect Σ2\Sigma_{2}. Then any point in X1\Σ1X_{1}\backslash\Sigma_{1} is also contained in some simple closed geodesic which does not intersect Σ1\Sigma_{1}.

Proof.

Observe that by assumption, Σ1\Sigma_{1} contains all the zeros of ω1\omega_{1}. Let xx be any point of X1\Σ1X_{1}\backslash\Sigma_{1}, then the image π⁡(x)\pi(x) of xx is a point of X2\Σ2X_{2}\backslash\Sigma_{2}. By assumption, π⁡(x)\pi(x) is contained in some simple closed geodesic γ\gamma such that γ∩Σ2=∅\gamma\cap\Sigma_{2}=\varnothing. On the other hand, the preimage of γ\gamma is a finite union of simple closed geodesics of (X1,ω1)(X_{1},\omega_{1}) which do not intersect Σ1\Sigma_{1}, one of which contains xx, say γ~\tilde{\gamma}. This completes the proof. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.

Let JJ be the set of regular points on (X,ω)(X,\omega) each of which is not contained in any simple closed geodesic. By Theorem 4.2, every point p∈Jp\in J is a periodic point of (X,ω)(X,\omega). By the work of Eskin-Filip-Wright [10, Theorem 1.5] (see also [7, Theorem 1.2]), (X,ω)(X,\omega) has infinitely many periodic points if and only if (X,ω)(X,\omega) is a torus cover. Thus Theorem 1 is proved for surfaces that are not torus covers.

Suppose now that (X,ω)(X,\omega) is a torus cover. Let

π:(X,ω)→(𝕋,{p1,…,pk})\pi:(X,\omega)\to(\mathbb{T},\{p_{1},\dots,p_{k}\})

be a translation cover, with (𝕋,{p1,…,pk})∈ℋ⁡(0k)(\mathbb{T},\{p_{1},\dots,p_{k}\})\in\mathcal{H}(0^{k}) for some k≥1k\geq 1. By Lemma 4.1, every regular point in 𝕋∖{p1,…,pk}\mathbb{T}\setminus\{p_{1},\dots,p_{k}\}, except for a finite set, is contained in some simple closed geodesic. Thus in this case, Theorem 1 is a direct consequence of Lemma 4.5. ∎

In this section, we prove Theorem 2.

Proof.

6. Regular Weierstrass points on surfaces in hyperelliptic components

In this section, we prove a technical result which is a generalization of [29, Lem. 2.1] and will be used in the proof of Theorem 3.

Proposition 6.1.

Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a translation surface belonging to a hyperelliptic component ℋhyp​(κ)\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(\kappa), where κ\kappa is either (2​g−2)(2g-2) or (g−1,g−1)(g-1,g-1) with g≥2g\geq 2. We denote by τ\tau the hyperelliptic involution of XX. Let II be a saddle connection on XX that is invariant by τ\tau. Then there exists a simple cylinder on XX that contains II.

For our purpose, we will need the following observation which is well known to experts in the field. We include its proof here for sake of completeness.

Lemma 6.2.

Let 𝐏=(P1​P2​P3​P4)\mathbf{P}=(P_{1}P_{2}P_{3}P_{4}) be a parallelogram in the plane. Assume that there is a continuous map φ:𝐏→X\varphi:\mathbf{P}\rightarrow X satisfying the following

  • ∙\bullet

    φ\varphi maps the vertices of 𝐏\mathbf{P} to the singularities of the flat metric,

  • ∙\bullet

    for any P∈𝐏∖{P1,P2,P3,P4}P\in\mathbf{P}\setminus\{P_{1},P_{2},P_{3},P_{4}\}, φ⁡(P)\varphi(P) is not a singularity,

  • ∙\bullet

    φ\varphi is locally isometric in int⁡(𝐏)\mathrm{int}(\mathbf{P}).

Then the restriction of φ\varphi to the interior of 𝐏\mathbf{P} is an embedding.

Remark 6.3.
  • •

    By assumption, φ\varphi maps the sides of 𝐏\mathbf{P} to some saddle connections of (X,ω)(X,\omega). It may happen that φ\varphi sends opposite sides of 𝐏\mathbf{P} to the same saddle connection.

  • •

    The assumption that no point in the interior of a side of 𝐏\mathbf{P} is mapped to a singularity is essential. For a counter example, consider a map from a rectangle in the plane onto a horizontal cylinder whose circumference is half of the length of the horizontal sides of the rectangle.

Proof of Lemma 6.2.

Without loss of generality, we can suppose that P1P_{1} is the origin of plane. Let u→\overrightarrow{u} and v→\overrightarrow{v} denote the vectors P1​P2→\overrightarrow{P_{1}P_{2}} and P1​P4→\overrightarrow{P_{1}P_{4}} respectively, then 𝐏={s​u→+t​v→,(s,t)∈[0;1]×[0;1]}\mathbf{P}=\{s\overrightarrow{u}+t\overrightarrow{v},\;(s,t)\in[0;1]\times[0;1]\}.

Assume now that there are two points P,P′∈int⁡(𝐏)P,P^{\prime}\in\mathrm{int}(\mathbf{P}) such that φ⁡(P)=φ⁡(P′)\varphi(P)=\varphi(P^{\prime}). Let w→\overrightarrow{w} denote the vector P​P′→\overrightarrow{PP^{\prime}}. We have w→=α​u→+β​v→\overrightarrow{w}=\alpha\overrightarrow{u}+\beta\overrightarrow{v}, with α,β∈(−1,1)×(−1,1)\alpha,\beta\in(-1;1)\times(-1;1). One can always find (a,b)∈{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)}(a,b)\in\{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)\} such that (α+a,β+b)∈[0;1)×[0;1)(\alpha+a,\beta+b)\in[0;1)\times[0;1). Namely, a=0a=0 if α≥0\alpha\geq 0 and a=1a=1 if α<0\alpha<0, b=0b=0 if β≥0\beta\geq 0 and b=1b=1 if β<0\beta<0. Note that α+a=0\alpha+a=0 only if α=0\alpha=0, and β+b=0\beta+b=0 only if β=0\beta=0. Since PP and P′P^{\prime} are two distinct points in the interior of 𝐏\mathbf{P}, we have (α,β)≠(0,0)(\alpha,\beta)\neq(0,0), which implies that (α+a,β+b)≠(0,0)(\alpha+a,\beta+b)\neq(0,0).

Let QQ be the point such that P1​Q→=(α+a)​u→+(β+b)​v→\overrightarrow{P_{1}Q}=(\alpha+a)\overrightarrow{u}+(\beta+b)\overrightarrow{v}. Since (α+a,β+b)∈[0;1)×[0;1)∖{(0,0)}(\alpha+a,\beta+b)\in[0;1)\times[0;1)\setminus\{(0,0)\}, the point QQ is located either in the interior of 𝐏\mathbf{P}, or in the interior of a side of 𝐏\mathbf{P}.

Let PiP_{i} be the vertex of 𝐏\mathbf{P} such that P1​Pi→=a​u→+b​v→\overrightarrow{P_{1}P_{i}}=a\overrightarrow{u}+b\overrightarrow{v}. Then

Pi​Q→=P1​Q→−P1​Pi→=α​u→+β​v→=P​P′→.\overrightarrow{P_{i}Q}=\overrightarrow{P_{1}Q}-\overrightarrow{P_{1}P_{i}}=\alpha\overrightarrow{u}+\beta\overrightarrow{v}=\overrightarrow{PP^{\prime}}.

Now since φ⁡(P)=φ⁡(P′)\varphi(P)=\varphi(P^{\prime}) and the holonomies of the flat metric are translations, the segments Pi​P¯\overline{P_{i}P} and Q​P′¯\overline{QP^{\prime}} are mapped to the same segment in XX, that is, the image of the parallelogram (P​P′​Q​Pi)(PP^{\prime}QP_{i}) (possibly degenerated) is contained in a cylinder. In particular, we must have φ⁡(Pi)=φ⁡(Q)\varphi(P_{i})=\varphi(Q). But by assumption φ⁡(Pi)\varphi(P_{i}) is a singularity while φ⁡(Q)\varphi(Q) is a regular point of the flat metric. We thus have a contradiction which proves the lemma. ∎

Recall that on a translation surface, a separatrix is a geodesic ray emanating from a singularity. In the proof of Proposition 6.1, we will repeatedly use the following two lemmas

Lemma 6.4.

Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a translation surface in a hyperelliptic component, and II be a horizontal saddle connection on XX which is invariant by the hyperelliptic involution. Assume that some vertical separatrices of XX intersect int⁡(I)\mathrm{int}(I). Then there is a parallelogram 𝐏\mathbf{P} in the plane, and a map φ:𝐏→X\varphi:\mathbf{P}\rightarrow X such that

  • (a)

    no side of 𝐏\mathbf{P} is vertical, nor horizontal,

  • (b)

    𝐏\mathbf{P} contains a horizontal diagonal which is mapped onto II.

  • (c)

    φ\varphi is locally isometric and maps each side of 𝐏\mathbf{P} to a saddle connection,

  • (d)

    the restriction of φ\varphi into int⁡(𝐏)\mathrm{int}(\mathbf{P}) is an embedding.

Proof.

Consider the set of vertical separatrices that intersect int⁡(I)\mathrm{int}(I). For each of these rays, we consider the segment from its origin to its first intersection with int⁡(I)\mathrm{int}(I). We then get a finite family of vertical geodesic segments, each of which joins a singularity to a point in int⁡(I)\mathrm{int}(I), and contains no point of int⁡(I)\mathrm{int}(I) in the interior. Let η\eta be a segment of minimal length in this family.

We can identify II with a horizontal segment P​Q¯\overline{PQ} in the plane, and η\eta with a vertical segment in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} whose endpoints are denoted be P1P_{1} and R1R_{1}, where R1∈int⁡(P​Q¯)R_{1}\in\mathrm{int}(\overline{PQ}). Let Q1Q_{1} denote the image of P1P_{1} under the rotation by π\pi around the midpoint of P​Q¯\overline{PQ}. Let 𝐏\mathbf{P} denote the parallelogram with vertices P,P1,Q,Q1P,P_{1},Q,Q_{1}.

Using the developing map (for instance by following the vertical lines through the points in P​Q¯\overline{PQ}), we can define a locally isometric map from a rectangle P​Q¯×(−ϵ,ϵ)\overline{PQ}\times(-\epsilon,\epsilon) to (X,ω)(X,\omega), for some ϵ>0\epsilon>0. We claim that this local isometry can be extended to the rectangle 𝐑\mathbf{R} (bounded by vertical and horizontal segments) that contains P,Q,P1,Q1P,Q,P_{1},Q_{1} in the boundary. Indeed, the extension to 𝐑\mathbf{R} fails only if there is a point in int⁡(𝐑)\mathrm{int}(\mathbf{R}) that gets mapped to a singularity of XX. But this implies that there is a vertical geodesic segment from that singularity to a point in int⁡(I)\mathrm{int}(I) which is shorter than η\eta. By the choice of η\eta, this is impossible.

Since 𝐏⊂𝐑\mathbf{P}\subset\mathbf{R}, we get a locally isometric map φ:𝐏→X\varphi:\mathbf{P}\rightarrow X. By construction, no side of 𝐏\mathbf{P} is vertical, nor horizontal, and we have φ⁡(P​Q¯)=I\varphi(\overline{PQ})=I.

Note that φ⁡(P​P1¯)\varphi(\overline{PP_{1}}) and φ⁡(Q​P1¯)\varphi(\overline{QP_{1}}) are saddle connections of (X,ω)(X,\omega) because P1P_{1} is mapped to a singularity. Since the hyperelliptic involution fixes the midpoint of II and permutes its endpoints, this involution can be identified with the rotation by π\pi around the midpoint of P​Q¯\overline{PQ} via φ\varphi. Consequently, φ⁡(Q1​Q¯)\varphi(\overline{Q_{1}Q}) and φ⁡(Q1​P¯)\varphi(\overline{Q_{1}P}) are also saddle connections of (X,ω)(X,\omega). It follows that the map φ\varphi satisfies the hypothesis of Lemma 6.2, hence the restriction of φ\varphi to int⁡(𝐏)\mathrm{int}(\mathbf{P}) is an embedding. ∎

Lemma 6.5.

Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a translation surface in a hyperelliptic component ℋhyp​(κ)\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(\kappa). Let (δ+,δ−)(\delta^{+},\delta^{-}) be a pair of saddle connections on XX that are permuted by the hyperelliptic involution τ\tau. Then removing δ+\delta^{+} and δ−\delta^{-} decomposes XX into two (connected) components invariant by τ\tau, the closures of these two components, denoted by X′X^{\prime} and X′′X^{\prime\prime}, are subsurfaces of XX bounded by δ+∪δ−\delta^{+}\cup\delta^{-}. The closed surfaces X^′\hat{X}^{\prime} and X^′′\hat{X}^{\prime\prime} obtained from X′X^{\prime} and X′′X^{\prime\prime} respectively by gluing δ+\delta^{+} and δ−\delta^{-} together belong to some hyperelliptic components of lower dimension than ℋhyp​(κ)\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(\kappa).

Proof.

By definition, there is a double cover π:X→𝕊2\pi:X\rightarrow\mathbb{S}^{2} branched over 2​g+22g+2 points (where gg is the genus of XX), and a quadratic differential qq on 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2} such that ω2=π∗​q\omega^{2}=\pi^{*}q. If g≥2g\geq 2 then qq has a unique zero and 2​g+12g+1 simple poles. For g=1g=1, qq has four simple poles. If κ=(0)\kappa=(0), then one of the poles is the image of the unique marked point of XX, and if κ=(0,0)\kappa=(0,0), then the image of the two marked points on XX is a regular marked point. By a slight abuse, in the case g=1g=1, we will consider the image of the marked point(s) on XX as the unique zero of qq. In all cases, let us denote by y0y_{0} the unique zero of qq.

Since δ+\delta^{+} and δ−\delta^{-} are permuted by τ\tau, both of them are mapped by π\pi onto a simple closed curve δ\delta through y0y_{0} on 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2}. Note that δ\delta is a saddle connection for the flat metric defined by qq. The curve δ\delta decomposes 𝕊2\mathbb{S}^{2} into two subsurfaces, denote by Y′,Y′′Y^{\prime},Y^{\prime\prime}, whose boundary is identified with δ\delta. Note that Y′Y^{\prime} and Y′′Y^{\prime\prime} are both homeomorphic to a closed disc.

Let X′=π−1​(Y′),X′′=π−1​(Y′′)X^{\prime}=\pi^{-1}(Y^{\prime}),X^{\prime\prime}=\pi^{-1}(Y^{\prime\prime}). Then X′X^{\prime} and X′′X^{\prime\prime} are connected subsurfaces of XX invariant under τ\tau whose boundary is δ+∪δ−\delta^{+}\cup\delta^{-}. This proves the first assertion of the lemma.

Let yy be the midpoint of δ\delta, that is, yy decomposes δ\delta into two subsegments δ1,δ2\delta_{1},\delta_{2} of the same length. Let Y^′\hat{Y}^{\prime} (resp. Y^′′\hat{Y}^{\prime\prime}) be the closed flat surface obtained from Y′Y^{\prime} (resp. Y′′Y^{\prime\prime}) by gluing δ1\delta_{1} and δ2\delta_{2} together so that yy becomes a singularity with cone angle equal to π\pi. Since Y^′\hat{Y}^{\prime} and Y^′′\hat{Y}^{\prime\prime} are homeomorphic to the sphere, and all the angles at the singularities of Y^′\hat{Y}^{\prime} and Y^′′\hat{Y}^{\prime\prime} are integral multiples of π\pi, the flat metric of Y^′\hat{Y}^{\prime} and Y^′′\hat{Y}^{\prime\prime} are defined by some quadratic differentials q′q^{\prime} and q′′q^{\prime\prime} respectively. By construction, q′q^{\prime} and q′′q^{\prime\prime} have at most one zero, which must be located at y0y_{0}.

It is not difficult to see that the surface X^′\hat{X}^{\prime} (resp. X^′′\hat{X}^{\prime\prime}) is actually the holonomy double cover of Y^′\hat{Y}^{\prime} (resp. Y^′′\hat{Y}^{\prime\prime}). Since q′q^{\prime} and q′′q^{\prime\prime} have at most one zero, X^′\hat{X}^{\prime} and X^′′\hat{X}^{\prime\prime} belong to some hyperelliptic components, and the second assertion of the lemma follows. ∎

Remark 6.6.

If XX is a hyperelliptic Riemann surface, but (X,ω)(X,\omega) does not belong to a hyperelliptic component, then the conclusion of Lemma 6.5 does not hold. This is because in this case qq has more than one zero, hence the image of δ+\delta^{+} and δ−\delta^{-} may be a simple arc on the sphere.

Proof of Proposition 6.1.

Without loss of generality, we can assume that II is horizontal. We identify II with a segment P​Q¯\overline{PQ} in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. It is a classical result that for all but countably many directions θ\theta, the flow in direction θ\theta is minimal on (X,ω)(X,\omega) (see for instance [22]). Pick a non-horizontal minimal direction θ\theta for (X,ω)(X,\omega). Using the action of {(1t01),t∈ℝ}\{\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&t\\ 0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right),\;t\in\mathbb{R}\}, we can assume that θ\theta is the vertical direction. Since the vertical flow is minimal, every vertical separatrix is dense in XX. In particular, they all intersect int⁡(I)\mathrm{int}(I).

Let 𝐏1=(P​P1​Q​Q1)\mathbf{P}_{1}=(PP_{1}QQ_{1}) be the parallelogram, and φ1:𝐏1→X\varphi_{1}:\mathbf{P}_{1}\rightarrow X be the locally isometric map constructed in Lemma 6.4. Let δ1+:=φ1​(P​P1¯)\delta_{1}^{+}:=\varphi_{1}(\overline{PP_{1}}), δ1−:=φ1​(Q1​Q¯)\delta^{-}_{1}:=\varphi_{1}(\overline{Q_{1}Q}), γ1+:=φ1​(Q​P1¯)\gamma^{+}_{1}:=\varphi_{1}(\overline{QP_{1}}), and γ1−:=φ1​(Q1​P¯)\gamma^{-}_{1}:=\varphi_{1}(\overline{Q_{1}P}). Note that δ1±\delta_{1}^{\pm} and γ1±\gamma_{1}^{\pm} are saddle connections of (X,ω)(X,\omega), and that δ1+\delta_{1}^{+} and δ1−\delta^{-}_{1} (resp. γ1+\gamma_{1}^{+} and γ1−\gamma_{1}^{-}) are exchanged by the hyperelliptic involution τ\tau.

If δ1+=δ1−\delta_{1}^{+}=\delta^{-}_{1} and γ1+=γ1−\gamma^{+}_{1}=\gamma^{-}_{1} then φ1​(𝐏1)\varphi_{1}(\mathbf{P}_{1}) is a closed torus, which is impossible since we have assumed that XX has genus at least two. Therefore, up to a relabeling of {P1,Q1}\{P_{1},Q_{1}\}, we can suppose that δ1+≠δ1−\delta_{1}^{+}\neq\delta_{1}^{-}.

We now consider the following algorithm: assume that we have a locally isometric map φn\varphi_{n} from a parallelogram 𝐏n=(P​Pn​Q​Qn)⊂ℝ2\mathbf{P}_{n}=(PP_{n}QQ_{n})\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} to XX that contains P​Q¯\overline{PQ} as a diagonal such that

  • (i)

    φn​(P​Q¯)=I\varphi_{n}(\overline{PQ})=I,

  • (ii)

    φn\varphi_{n} maps the sides of 𝐏n\mathbf{P}_{n} to saddle connections of (X,ω)(X,\omega),

  • (iii)

    the restriction of φn\varphi_{n} to the interior of 𝐏n\mathbf{P}_{n} is an embedding,

  • (iv)

    δn+:=φn​(P​Pn¯)\delta^{+}_{n}:=\varphi_{n}(\overline{PP_{n}}) and δn−:=φn​(Q​Qn¯)\delta^{-}_{n}:=\varphi_{n}(\overline{QQ_{n}}) are two different saddle connections.

Let us denote by γn+\gamma^{+}_{n} and γn−\gamma^{-}_{n} the saddle connections of (X,ω)(X,\omega) which are the images of Q​Pn¯\overline{QP_{n}} and P​Qn¯\overline{PQ_{n}} under φn\varphi_{n} respectively.

If γn+=γn−\gamma^{+}_{n}=\gamma^{-}_{n} then the algorithm stops. In this case, φn​(𝐏n)\varphi_{n}(\mathbf{P}_{n}) is a simple cylinder (bounded by δn+\delta^{+}_{n} and δn−\delta^{-}_{n}) that contains II and we are done. Otherwise, we use the action of a matrix Ut=(1t01),t∈ℝU_{t}=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&t\\ 0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right),t\in\mathbb{R}, to make P​Pn¯\overline{PP_{n}} a vertical segment. By a slight abuse of notation, we continue denoting by 𝐏n\mathbf{P}_{n} and (X,ω)(X,\omega) the images of 𝐏n\mathbf{P}_{n} and of (X,ω)(X,\omega) under the action of UtU_{t} respectively. Consequently, there is a map from 𝐏n\mathbf{P}_{n} to (X,ω)(X,\omega) with the same properties as φn\varphi_{n}. We denote this map also by φn\varphi_{n}. It is worth noticing that, even though in each step we actually change the surface (X,ω)(X,\omega) by applying to it some matrix in {(1t01),t∈ℝ}\{\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&t\\ 0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right),\;t\in\mathbb{R}\}, the conclusion we get also holds for the original surface because we are staying in the same GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})-orbit.

We then have two cases:

  • ∙\bullet

    Case 1: some vertical separatrices intersect int⁡(I)\mathrm{int}(I). In this case, using Lemma 6.4, we obtain a locally isometric map φn+1\varphi_{n+1} from parallelogram 𝐏n+1=(P​Pn+1​Q​Qn+1)\mathbf{P}_{n+1}=(PP_{n+1}QQ_{n+1}), that contains P​Q¯\overline{PQ} as a diagonal to XX. We choose the labeling such that Pn+1P_{n+1} and PnP_{n} are on the same side with respect to II (see Figure 3).

    By construction, φn+1\varphi_{n+1} satisfies the properties (i),(ii), (iii). We claim that φn+1\varphi_{n+1} satisfies (iv) as well. Let δn+1+:=φn+1​(P​Pn+1¯)\delta^{+}_{n+1}:=\varphi_{n+1}(\overline{PP_{n+1}}) and δn+1−:=φn+1​(Q​Qn+1¯)\delta^{-}_{n+1}:=\varphi_{n+1}(\overline{QQ_{n+1}}). Suppose that δn+1+=δn+1−\delta^{+}_{n+1}=\delta^{-}_{n+1}. Because P​Pn+1¯\overline{PP_{n+1}} and Qn+1​Q¯\overline{Q_{n+1}Q} are mapped to the same saddle connections, the geodesic rays in direction (0,1)(0,1) starting from PP and from Qn+1Q_{n+1} are mapped to the same ray in XX. Let Q′Q^{\prime} be the point in the plane such that Qn+1​Q′→=P​Pn→\overrightarrow{Q_{n+1}Q^{\prime}}=\overrightarrow{PP_{n}}.

    If Q′∈int⁡(𝐏n+1)Q^{\prime}\in\mathrm{int}(\mathbf{P}_{n+1}) then φn+1​(Qn+1​Q′¯)=δn+\varphi_{n+1}(\overline{Q_{n+1}Q^{\prime}})=\delta_{n}^{+}, but this is a contradiction because points in int⁡(𝐏n+1)\mathrm{int}(\mathbf{P}_{n+1}) are mapped to regular points in XX. Thus Q′∉int⁡(𝐏n+1)Q^{\prime}\not\in\mathrm{int}(\mathbf{P}_{n+1}). Consequently, the segment Qn+1​Q′¯\overline{Q_{n+1}Q^{\prime}} must intersect int⁡(P​Q¯)\mathrm{int}(\overline{PQ}), which implies that δn+\delta_{n}^{+} intersects int⁡(I)\mathrm{int}(I) contradicting the hypothesis that φn\varphi_{n} is an embedding in int⁡(𝐏n)\mathrm{int}(\mathbf{P}_{n}). Therefore, we must have δn+1+≠δn+1−\delta_{n+1}^{+}\neq\delta_{n+1}^{-}.

  • ∙\bullet

    Case 2: no vertical separatrix intersects int⁡(I)\mathrm{int}(I). In this case II is contained in a vertical cylinder VV whose boundary contains δn+\delta^{+}_{n} and δn−\delta^{-}_{n}. Let ℓ\ell be the circumference of VV. We can represent VV by a rectangle 𝐑=(P​Q​Q′​P′)\mathbf{R}=(PQQ^{\prime}P^{\prime}) in the plane as shown in Figure 3, where the length of P​P′¯\overline{PP^{\prime}} and Q​Q′¯\overline{QQ^{\prime}} is ℓ\ell. There is a locally isometric mapping φ:𝐑→X\varphi:\mathbf{R}\rightarrow X such that φ⁡(P​Q¯)=φ⁡(P′​Q′¯)=I\varphi(\overline{PQ})=\varphi(\overline{P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}})=I, and the restriction of φ\varphi to int⁡(𝐑)\mathrm{int}(\mathbf{R}) is an embedding.

    The vertical sides of 𝐑\mathbf{R} are decomposed into several segments, each of which is mapped to a saddle connection of (X,ω)(X,\omega). By construction P​Pn¯\overline{PP_{n}} is the bottom most segment in the left border of 𝐑\mathbf{R}. Let Qn′Q^{\prime}_{n} be the lower endpoint of the topmost segment in the right border of 𝐑\mathbf{R}, then Q′​Qn′¯\overline{Q^{\prime}Q^{\prime}_{n}} is mapped to the saddle connection δn−\delta^{-}_{n}.

    If VV is a simple cylinder then γn+=γn−\gamma_{n}^{+}=\gamma_{n}^{-} and we are done. Thus, let us suppose that the left border of VV contains a saddle connection other than δn+\delta^{+}_{n}. Since VV is invariant under the hyperelliptic involution (because II is), its right border must contain the same number of saddle connections as its left border. Therefore, the right border must contain a saddle connection other than δn−\delta^{-}_{n}.

    Let Qn+1′Q^{\prime}_{n+1} be the lower endpoint of the topmost segment in the left border of 𝐑\mathbf{R}, and Pn+1P_{n+1} be the upper endpoint of the bottommost segment in the right border of 𝐑\mathbf{R}. Then the saddle connection which is the image of P′​Qn+1′¯\overline{P^{\prime}Q^{\prime}_{n+1}} is not δn+\delta^{+}_{n}, and the one which is the image of Q​Pn+1¯\overline{QP_{n+1}} is not δn−\delta^{-}_{n}.

    Let Qn+1Q_{n+1} be the image of Qn+1′Q^{\prime}_{n+1} under the translation by P′​P→\overrightarrow{P^{\prime}P}. Consider the parallelogram 𝐏n+1=(P​Pn+1​Q​Qn+1)\mathbf{P}_{n+1}=(PP_{n+1}QQ_{n+1}). The map from 𝐑\mathbf{R} to (X,ω)(X,\omega) can be extended to the triangle (P​Q​Qn+1)(PQQ_{n+1}), hence we have a locally isometric map φn+1:𝐏n+1→(X,ω)\varphi_{n+1}:\mathbf{P}_{n+1}\rightarrow(X,\omega). Let us denote by δn+1+\delta^{+}_{n+1} and δn+1−\delta^{-}_{n+1} the images under φn+1\varphi_{n+1} of P​Pn+1¯\overline{PP_{n+1}} and Q​Qn+1¯\overline{QQ_{n+1}} respectively. It is straightforward to check that φn+1\varphi_{n+1} satisfies the properties (i),…,(iv).

We now show that the algorithm has to stop after finitely many steps. For i∈{n,n+1}i\in\{n,n+1\}, since δi+\delta^{+}_{i} and δi−\delta^{-}_{i} are permuted by τ\tau, it follows from Lemma 6.5 that (δi+,δi−)(\delta^{+}_{i},\delta^{-}_{i}) decomposes XX into two subsurfaces invariant by τ\tau. Let XiX_{i} denote the subsurface that contains II.

Let ϑ⁡(Xi)\vartheta(X_{i}) be the total cone angle at the singularities of XX inside XiX_{i}. To be more precise, if ω\omega has one zero, then δi+,δi−\delta_{i}^{+},\delta_{i}^{-} divide a small disk about the unique zero of ω\omega into 4 sectors. In this case ϑ⁡(Xi)\vartheta(X_{i}) is the sum of the angles of the two sectors contained in XiX_{i}. If ω\omega has two zeros, then δi+,δi−\delta^{+}_{i},\delta^{-}_{i} give two rays at each zero. In this case ϑ⁡(Xi)\vartheta(X_{i}) is the sum of the angles of the sectors (one at each zero) that are contained in XiX_{i}.

Note that ϑ⁡(Xi)\vartheta(X_{i}) is also the total angle at the singularities of the translation surface X^i\hat{X}_{i} which is obtained from XiX_{i} by gluing δi+\delta^{+}_{i} and δi−\delta^{-}_{i} together. Therefore, ϑ⁡(Xi)\vartheta(X_{i}) must be an integral multiple of 2​π2\pi. Note also that ϑ⁡(Xi)=2​π\vartheta(X_{i})=2\pi if and only if XiX_{i} is a simple cylinder, in which case X^i\hat{X}_{i} is a torus with a marked point.

If δn+\delta^{+}_{n} and δn+1+\delta^{+}_{n+1} intersect at a point in their interior, then there is a point in int⁡(P​Pn+1¯)\mathrm{int}(\overline{PP_{n+1}}) which is mapped to a point in δn+\delta^{+}_{n}. By considering the vertical ray starting from this point in direction (0,−1)(0,-1), we see that δn+\delta^{+}_{n} must intersect int⁡(I)\mathrm{int}(I). This is because this vertical ray must terminate at a singularity, but all the points in int⁡(𝐏n+1)\mathrm{int}(\mathbf{P}_{n+1}) are mapped to regular points of XX, hence it must cross 𝐏n+1\mathbf{P}_{n+1} entirely. In particular it must intersect int⁡(P​Q¯)\mathrm{int}(\overline{PQ}). Since this contradicts the assumption that φn\varphi_{n} is an embedding in int⁡(𝐏n)\mathrm{int}(\mathbf{P}_{n}), we conclude that δn+1+\delta^{+}_{n+1} and δn+\delta^{+}_{n} can only meet at their endpoints. Similarly, δn+1−\delta^{-}_{n+1} and δn+\delta^{+}_{n} can only meet at their endpoints as well. Since δn−\delta^{-}_{n} is the image of δn+\delta^{+}_{n} under the hyperelliptic involution, the same statements hold for δn−\delta^{-}_{n}.

It follows that Xn+1X_{n+1} is a proper subsurface of XnX_{n}, and therefore ϑ⁡(Xn+1)<ϑ⁡(Xn)\vartheta(X_{n+1})<\vartheta(X_{n}). Consequently, the algorithm has to stop after at most ϑ⁡(X)/(2​π)\vartheta(X)/(2\pi) steps, where ϑ⁡(X)\vartheta(X) is the total cone angle at the singularity of XX, and we get a simple cylinder that contains II. ∎

Corollary 6.7.

Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a translation surface in some hyperelliptic component ℋhyp​(κ)\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(\kappa) of genus at least 22. Let WW be a Weierstrass point of XX which is not a zero of ω\omega. Then WW is contained in a simple cylinder of (X,ω)(X,\omega).

Proof.

Let JJ be a geodesic segment of that realizes the distance from WW to the zero set of ω\omega. Then I:=J∪τ⁡(J)I:=J\cup\tau(J) is a saddle connection invariant by τ\tau. Thus, by Proposition 6.1, there is a simple cylinder CC in XX that contains II. ∎

7. Proof of Theorem 3

In this section, we will prove Theorem 3. Let ℒ\mathcal{L} be the GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit closure of (X,ω)(X,\omega) in ℋhyp​(κ)\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(\kappa) with κ∈{(2​g−2),(g−1,g−1)},g≥2\kappa\in\{(2g-2),(g-1,g-1)\},\;g\geq 2. By Theorem 2.9, there are five possibilities:

  1. (I)

    ℒ=ℋhyp​(κ)\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(\kappa), where κ=(2​g−2)\kappa=(2g-2) or (g−1,g−1)(g-1,g-1).

  2. (II)

    4≤dimℒ<dimℋhyp​(κ)4\leq\dim\mathcal{L}<\dim\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(\kappa) and ℒ\mathcal{L} is obtained from a translation covering construction over ℋhyp​(κ′)\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(\kappa^{\prime}), that is, surfaces in ℒ\mathcal{L} are translation covers of surfaces in ℋhyp​(κ′)\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(\kappa^{\prime}), where κ′=(2​r−2)\kappa^{\prime}=(2r-2) or (r−1,r−1)(r-1,r-1) and 2≤r<g2\leq r<g. In this case, we will write ℒ=ℋhyp~​(κ′)\mathcal{L}=\widetilde{\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}}(\kappa^{\prime}).

  3. (III)

    dimℒ=3\dim\mathcal{L}=3 and ℒ\mathcal{L} consists of translation covers of surfaces in some eigenform locus Ω​ED​(1,1)\Omega E_{D}(1,1) in ℋ⁡(1,1)\mathcal{H}(1,1), where the associated discriminant DD is not a square. In this case we will write ℒ=Ω​E~D​(1,1)\mathcal{L}=\widetilde{\Omega E}_{D}(1,1).

  4. (IV)

    dimℒ=3\dim\mathcal{L}=3 and ℒ\mathcal{L} consists of translation covers of surfaces in ℋ⁡(0,0)\mathcal{H}(0,0), the covering maps are ramified over two points. In this case we will write ℒ=ℋ~​(0,0)\mathcal{L}=\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}(0,0).

  5. (V)

    dimℒ=2\dim\mathcal{L}=2, ℒ\mathcal{L} is a closed orbit.

Remark 7.1.
  • •

    Case (4) and (5) in Theorem 2.9 are regrouped in Case (II) above.

  • •

    The numbering is chosen to better fit the strategy of the proof.

7.1. Case I: ℒ=ℋhyp​(κ)\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(\kappa)

Proof of Theorem 3 for Case I.

Suppose to a contradiction that there is a regular point pp of (X,ω)(X,\omega) which is not contained in any closed geodesic. By Theorem 4.2, pp is a periodic point of (X,ω)(X,\omega). Therefore, pp is a Weierstrass point of (X,ω)(X,\omega) by Theorem 2.11. But by Corollary 6.7, pp is contained in a simple cylinder. Thus we have a contradiction, which proves the theorem for this case. ∎

7.2. Case II: ℒ=ℋhyp~​(κ′)\mathcal{L}=\widetilde{\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}}(\kappa^{\prime}) for some κ′=(2​r−2)\kappa^{\prime}=(2r-2) or (r−1,r−1)(r-1,r-1) with 2≤r<g2\leq r<g

Proof of Theorem 3 for Case II.

Let π:(X,ω)→(X′,ω′)\pi:(X,\omega)\to(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime}) be a translation cover with (X′,ω′)∈ℋhyp​(κ′)(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime})\in{\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(\kappa^{\prime})}. Let Σ\Sigma and Σ′\Sigma^{\prime} be the zero sets of ω\omega and ω′\omega^{\prime} respectively. In this case we have Σ=π−1​(Σ′)\Sigma=\pi^{-1}(\Sigma^{\prime}). By assumption, the GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit closure of (X′,ω′)(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime}) is ℋhyp​(κ′){\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(\kappa^{\prime})}. By Theorem 3 for Case I, any regular point of (X′,ω′)(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime}) is contained in infinitely many simple closed geodesics. Lemma 4.5 then implies that the same is true for (X,ω)(X,\omega). ∎

7.3. Case III: ℒ=Ω​E~D​(1,1)\mathcal{L}=\widetilde{\Omega E}_{D}(1,1), DD is not a square.

Proof of Theorem 3 for Case III.

Let π:(X,ω)→(Y,η)∈Ω​ED​(1,1)\pi:(X,\omega)\to(Y,\eta)\in{\Omega E_{D}(1,1)} be a translation cover which is branched over the zeros of η\eta. Then GL​(2,ℝ)⋅(Y,η)¯=Ω​ED​(1,1)\overline{\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})\cdot(Y,\eta)}={\Omega E_{D}(1,1)}. By Lemma 4.5, to prove Theorem 3, it suffices to prove that every regular point of (Y,η)(Y,\eta) is contained in some simple closed geodesic of (Y,η)(Y,\eta). Suppose to a contradiction that (Y,η)(Y,\eta) contains a regular point qq which is not contained in any simple closed geodesic. Then, by Theorem 4.2, qq is a periodic point of (Y,η)(Y,\eta). If qq is a Weierstrass point, by Corollary 6.7, qq is contained in a simple cylinder and we have a contradiction.

If qq is not a Weierstrass point of (Y,η)(Y,\eta), then by Theorem 2.11, GL​(2,ℝ)⋅(Y,η)¯\overline{\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R})\cdot(Y,\eta)} is the golden eigenform locus. It follows from [6, Sect. 2], that the GL​(2,ℝ)\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}) orbit closure of (Y,η,q)(Y,\eta,q) contains a marked translation surface (Y′,η′,q′)(Y^{\prime},\eta^{\prime},q^{\prime}), where (Y′,η′)(Y^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}) is a Veech surface, and q′q^{\prime} is a regular Weierstrass point. By Lemma 4.4, q′q^{\prime} is not contained in any simple closed geodesic of (Y′,η′)(Y^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}), which again contradicts Corollary 6.7. ∎

Remark 7.2.

For this case, the theorem can also be shown by more direct arguments, using the fact that surfaces in eigenform loci are completely periodic in the sense of Calta.

7.4. Case V: ℒ\mathcal{L} is a closed orbit, that is (X,ω)(X,\omega) is a Veech surface

Let us start with the following observation

Lemma 7.3.

Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a translation surface in ℋhyp​(2​g−2)\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(2g-2) or ℋhyp​(g−1,g−1)\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(g-1,g-1). Let γ\gamma be a saddle connection of (X,ω)(X,\omega) which is invariant under the hyperelliptic involution. Assume that γ\gamma is contained in the boundary of a cylinder CC. Then γ\gamma is contained in a simple cylinder DD such that D⊂C¯D\subset\overline{C}, and the core curves of DD cross CC once.

Proof.

Applying a rotation if necessary, we can assume that CC is horizontal. Without loss of generality , we can assume that γ\gamma is contained in the top boundary of CC. Since (X,ω)(X,\omega) belongs to a hyperelliptic component, CC is invariant under the hyperelliptic involution (see for instance [19, 30]). This implies that γ\gamma is also contained in the bottom boundary of CC. Therefore, there are (infinitely many) simple closed geodesics in C¯\overline{C} that join the midpoint of γ\gamma to itself and cross every core curve of CC once. The cylinder corresponding to any such closed geodesic has the required properties. ∎

We now show

Proposition 7.4.

Let (X,ω)(X,\omega) be a Veech surface in ℋhyp​(κ)\mathcal{H}^{\rm hyp}(\kappa) where κ=(2​g−2)\kappa=(2g-2) or (g−1,g−1)(g-1,g-1). Then every regular point in (X,ω)(X,\omega) is contained in some simple closed geodesic.

Proof.

Step 1. Let ww be a regular Weierstrass point, let JJ be a geodesic segment of that realizes the distance from ww to the zero set of ω\omega. Then γ0:=J∪τ⁡(J)\gamma_{0}:=J\cup\tau(J) is a saddle connection invariant by τ\tau. Since (X,ω)(X,\omega) is a Veech surface, it is periodic in the direction of γ0\gamma_{0}. Thus γ0\gamma_{0} is contained in the boundary of some cylinder C0C_{0}. By Lemma 7.3, there is a simple cylinder D0D_{0} in C¯0\overline{C}_{0} that contains γ0\gamma_{0}. Let γ1+,γ1−\gamma^{+}_{1},\gamma^{-}_{1} be the two saddle connections bordering D0D_{0}. Then the saddle connections γ0,γ1+,γ1−\gamma_{0},\gamma^{+}_{1},\gamma^{-}_{1} bound an embedded parallelogram P0P_{0}. By construction every regular point in P¯0\overline{P}_{0} is contained in a closed geodesic (regular points in γ1±\gamma^{\pm}_{1} and in int⁡(P0)\mathrm{int}(P_{0}) are contained in C0C_{0}, while regular points in γ0\gamma_{0} are contained in D0D_{0}).

Step 2. Note that the hyperelliptic involution preserves D0D_{0}, exchanges γ1+\gamma^{+}_{1} and γ1−\gamma^{-}_{1}, hence it preserves the complement of D0D_{0}. Remove int⁡(D0)\mathrm{int}(D_{0}) from XX and identify γ1+\gamma^{+}_{1} with γ1−\gamma^{-}_{1}, we get a closed translation surface (X1,ω1)(X_{1},\omega_{1}) in some hyperelliptic component of lower dimension (c.f. Lemma 6.5). Let γ1\gamma_{1} denote the saddle connection corresponding to γ1+\gamma^{+}_{1} and γ1−\gamma^{-}_{1} on X1X_{1}. Then γ1\gamma_{1} is invariant under the hyperelliptic involution of (X1,ω1)(X_{1},\omega_{1}).

Since (X,ω)(X,\omega) is a Veech surface, it is periodic in the direction of γ1±\gamma^{\pm}_{1}. Therefore, (X1,ω1)(X_{1},\omega_{1}) is periodic in this direction. It follows that γ1\gamma_{1} is contained in the boundary of a cylinder C1C_{1} of (X1,ω1)(X_{1},\omega_{1}). Again by Lemma 7.3, γ1\gamma_{1} is contained in a simple cylinder D1⊂C¯1D_{1}\subset\overline{C}_{1} bounded by two saddle connections γ2+,γ2−\gamma^{+}_{2},\gamma^{-}_{2}. By construction every point in int⁡(γ2+)∪int⁡(γ2−)\mathrm{int}(\gamma^{+}_{2})\cup\mathrm{int}(\gamma^{-}_{2}) is contained in C1C_{1}.

In XX, D1D_{1} corresponds to an embedded parallelogram P1P_{1} which is bounded by γ1±\gamma^{\pm}_{1} and γ2±\gamma^{\pm}_{2}. By construction, every regular point in P¯1\overline{P}_{1} is contained in a simple closed geodesic of (X,ω)(X,\omega).

Step 3. By repeating Step 2, we get a sequence of pairs of saddle connections (γi+,γi−),i=1,2,…(\gamma_{i}^{+},\gamma_{i}^{-}),\;i=1,2,\dots as follows: in the ii-th step, we have a pair of saddle connections (γi+,γi−)(\gamma^{+}_{i},\gamma^{-}_{i}) permuted by the hyperelliptic involution that decompose XX into two components (c.f. Lemma 6.5), one of which contains γ0\gamma_{0} and all the pairs (γ1+,γ1−),…,(γi−1+,γi−1−)(\gamma^{+}_{1},\gamma^{-}_{1}),\dots,(\gamma^{+}_{i-1},\gamma^{-}_{i-1}). Consider the other component. Its closure is a subsurface of XX bounded by γi+∪γi−\gamma^{+}_{i}\cup\gamma^{-}_{i}. Denote by (Xi,ωi)(X_{i},\omega_{i}) the translation surface obtained from this subsurface by gluing γi+\gamma^{+}_{i} and γi−\gamma^{-}_{i} together. By Lemma 6.5, (Xi,ωi)(X_{i},\omega_{i}) belongs to some hyperelliptic component. Note that the identification of γi+\gamma^{+}_{i} and γi−\gamma^{-}_{i} gives rise to a saddle connection γi\gamma_{i} in XiX_{i} that is invariant by the hyperelliptic involution.

Since (X,ω)(X,\omega) is a Veech surface, the direction of γi±\gamma^{\pm}_{i} is periodic. Recall that Xi∖γiX_{i}\setminus\gamma_{i} is a subsurface of XX, therefore XiX_{i} is decomposed into cylinders in the direction of γi\gamma_{i}. Since (Xi,ωi)(X_{i},\omega_{i}) is in a hyperelliptic component, there is a unique cylinder CiC_{i} in this family that contains γi\gamma_{i} it its boundary. By Lemma 7.3, γi\gamma_{i} is contained in a simple cylinder DiD_{i} whose every core curve crosses CiC_{i} once. The two saddle connections in the boundary of DiD_{i} are the pair (γi+1+,γi+1−)(\gamma^{+}_{i+1},\gamma^{-}_{i+1}) in our sequence. Note that, since γi+1±\gamma^{\pm}_{i+1} do not intersect γi\gamma_{i} in its interior, γi+1+,γi+1−\gamma^{+}_{i+1},\gamma^{-}_{i+1} are actually saddle connections in (X,ω)(X,\omega).

By construction, γi+1+,γi+1−,γi+,γi−\gamma^{+}_{i+1},\gamma^{-}_{i+1},\gamma^{+}_{i},\gamma^{-}_{i} bound an embedded parallelogram PiP_{i} in XX. Since int⁡(Pi)\mathrm{int}(P_{i}) is contained in int⁡(Ci)\mathrm{int}(C_{i}), every point in int⁡(Pi)\mathrm{int}(P_{i}) is contained in a core curve of CiC_{i}. The same is true for every point in int⁡(γi+1+)\mathrm{int}(\gamma^{+}_{i+1}) and in int⁡(γi+1−)\mathrm{int}(\gamma^{-}_{i+1}).

Observe that the embedded parallelograms obtained from this procedure are pairwise disjoint (see Figure 4). Since the total angle in a parallelogram is 2​π2\pi, the procedure must stop after ϑ⁡(X)/(2​π)\vartheta(X)/(2\pi) iterations, where ϑ⁡(X)\vartheta(X) is the total cone angle at the singularities of XX, and we get a decomposition of XX into parallelograms. Since any regular point in the closure of each parallelogram in this decomposition is contained in at least one simple closed geodesic, the proposition follows. ∎

Proof of Theorem 3 Case V.

In this case, Theorem 3 is a direct consequence of Proposition 7.4 and Theorem 2. ∎

7.5. Case IV: ℒ=ℋ~​(0,0)\mathcal{L}=\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}(0,0)

Proof of Theorem 3 for Case IV.

Recall that in this case ω\omega must have two zeros. We first notice that there is a map F:ℒ→ℋ⁡(0,0)F:\mathcal{L}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}(0,0) defined as follows: given (X,ω)∈ℒ(X,\omega)\in\mathcal{L}, let Λω:={∫cω,c∈H1​(X,ℤ)}\Lambda_{\omega}:=\{\int_{c}\omega,\;c\in H_{1}(X,\mathbb{Z})\}. Then Λω\Lambda_{\omega} is a lattice in ℂ\mathbb{C}. Thus 𝕋:=ℂ/Λω\mathbb{T}:=\mathbb{C}/\Lambda_{\omega} is a torus. Pick a base point p0∈Xp_{0}\in X and define a map π:X→𝕋\pi:X\rightarrow\mathbb{T} by π⁡(q)=∫p0qω​ mod ​Λω\pi(q)=\int_{p_{0}}^{q}\omega\text{ mod }\Lambda_{\omega} for any q∈Xq\in X, where the integration is taken along any path from p0p_{0} to qq. It is not difficult to see that π\pi is well defined. Let x1,x2x_{1},x_{2} be the images of the zeros of ω\omega under π\pi. We define F⁡((X,ω))=(𝕋,{x1,x2})∈ℋ⁡(0,0)F((X,\omega))=(\mathbb{T},\{x_{1},x_{2}\})\in\mathcal{H}(0,0). By construction π:(X,ω)→(𝕋,{x1,x2})\pi:(X,\omega)\rightarrow(\mathbb{T},\{x_{1},x_{2}\}) is a translation cover which is branched over {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\}.

Let pp be a regular point on XX. Assume that π⁡(p)∉{x1,x2}\pi(p)\not\in\{x_{1},x_{2}\}. By Lemma 4.1, there is a closed geodesic γ\gamma through π⁡(p)\pi(p) which does not intersect the set {x1,x2}\{x_{1},x_{2}\}. Then the component of π−1​(γ)\pi^{-1}(\gamma) that contains pp is a closed geodesic of (X,ω)(X,\omega) (c.f. Lemma 4.5) so we are done.

Assume now that π⁡(p)∈{x1,x2}\pi(p)\in\{x_{1},x_{2}\}, say π⁡(p)=x1\pi(p)=x_{1}. In this case, given a closed geodesic γ⊂𝕋\gamma\subset\mathbb{T} through π⁡(p)\pi(p), the component of π−1​(γ)\pi^{-1}(\gamma) that contains pp may also contain the zero of ω\omega that projects to x1x_{1}. To prove the theorem in this case, we will make use of Case V, which has been proved.

Suppose to a contradiction that pp is not contained in any simple closed geodesic of (X,ω)(X,\omega). Recall that the set of square-tiled surfaces is dense in ℒ\mathcal{L}. Let (X′,ω′)∈ℒ(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime})\in\mathcal{L} be a square-tiled surface, and π′:(X′,ω′)→(𝕋′,{x1′,x2′})\pi^{\prime}:(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime})\to(\mathbb{T}^{\prime},\{x_{1}^{\prime},x_{2}^{\prime}\}) a translation cover where (𝕋′,{x1′,x2′})∈ℋ⁡(0,0)(\mathbb{T}^{\prime},\{x^{\prime}_{1},x^{\prime}_{2}\})\in\mathcal{H}(0,0) is the image of (X′,ω′)(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime}) under FF. Note that the condition (X′,ω′)(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime}) is square-tiled means that x1′−x2′x^{\prime}_{1}-x^{\prime}_{2} is a torsion point of 𝕋′\mathbb{T}^{\prime}.

By assumption, there exist an∈GL​(2,ℝ),n∈ℕa_{n}\in\textup{GL}(2,\mathbb{R}),\;n\in\mathbb{N}, such that an⋅(X,ω)→(X′,ω′)a_{n}\cdot(X,\omega)\to(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime}) as n→∞n\to\infty. Let (Xn,ωn,pn):=an⋅(X,ω,p)(X_{n},\omega_{n},p_{n}):=a_{n}\cdot(X,\omega,p), (𝕋n,{x1​n,x2​n}):=an⋅(𝕋,{x1,x2})(\mathbb{T}_{n},\{x_{1n},x_{2n}\}):=a_{n}\cdot(\mathbb{T},\{x_{1},x_{2}\}), and πn:(Xn,ωn)→(𝕋n,{x1​n,x2​n})\pi_{n}:(X_{n},\omega_{n})\to(\mathbb{T}_{n},\{x_{1n},x_{2n}\}) the corresponding translation covers. Since the map FF is continuous, (𝕋n,{x1​n,x2​n})(\mathbb{T}_{n},\{x_{1n},x_{2n}\}) converges to (𝕋′,{x1′,x2′})(\mathbb{T}^{\prime},\{x_{1}^{\prime},x_{2}^{\prime}\}) as n→∞n\to\infty.

There exists some positive constant δ\delta such that any two points in (π′)−1​({x1′,x2′})⊂X′(\pi^{\prime})^{-1}(\{x_{1}^{\prime},x_{2}^{\prime}\})\subset X^{\prime} are of distance at least δ\delta away from each other with respect to the flat metric defined by ω′\omega^{\prime}. Therefore, there exists a constant N>0N>0, such that for all n>Nn>N, pnp_{n} is of distance at least δ/2\delta/2 away from any zero of ωn\omega_{n} (with respect to the flat metric defined by ωn\omega_{n}), since pn∈πn−1​({x1​n,x2​n})p_{n}\in\pi_{n}^{-1}(\{x_{1n},x_{2n}\}).

After passing to a subsequence if necessary, we have (Xn,ωn,pn)(X_{n},\omega_{n},p_{n}) converges to (X′,ω′,p′)(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime},p^{\prime}) as n→∞n\to\infty, where p′∈(π′)−1​({x1′,x2′})p^{\prime}\in(\pi^{\prime})^{-1}(\{x_{1}^{\prime},x_{2}^{\prime}\}) is a regular point. By Lemma 4.4, p′p^{\prime} is not contained in any simple closed geodesic of (X′,ω′)(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime}), which contradicts Theorem 3 for Case V, since (X′,ω′)(X^{\prime},\omega^{\prime}) is a Veech surface. Thus Theorem 3 holds for Case IV. The proof of Theorem 3 is now complete. ∎

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
